cues.text: A Wandering Early Life
Born João Cidade in 1495 at Montemor-o-Novo in Portugal, John lived a restless early life as a shepherd and then a soldier.
He served in various military campaigns across Europe before drifting into a period as a bookseller in Granada, Spain—a life so far marked more by wandering than by settled purpose.
A Dramatic Conversion
In his fortieth year, moved profoundly by a sermon of the celebrated preacher St. John of Ávila , John underwent a sudden and overwhelming conversion.

Its outward expression was so intense — weeping, self-accusation, and dramatic penance — that he was for a time confined to a hospital for the mentally ill, where he continued to serve the other patients amid his own confinement.
Founding a Hospital in Granada
Once released and counseled by John of Ávila to channel his zeal into concrete works of charity, John rented a house in Granada.
He began personally caring for the sick poor, soliciting supplies and alms by night and tending patients by day.
His tireless, hands-on devotion soon drew the cooperation of sympathetic priests and physicians, and the modest house grew into a proper hospital.
The Name Given by Christ
Tradition holds that Christ himself appeared to John, expressing pleasure with his work.
He told John he wished him to be known as 'John of God.'
The Bishop of Tuy wished to curb John's habit of giving away his own cloak to any beggar he encountered.
He had a distinctive religious habit made for John—the garment that became, in its essentials, the habit of the order that would bear his name.
Rescuing the Sick from Fire
Among the many miracles attributed to John, one of the best-known traditional accounts is his rescue of patients from the Royal Hospital of Granada during a devastating fire.
Commemorated in the official liturgical texts of his feast, John himself is said to have walked through the flames unharmed while carrying the sick to safety.
Legacy
John died at Granada on March 8, 1550, having spent roughly a decade in this intense ministry of hospital care.

His companions and followers organized formally into the Brothers Hospitallers of St. John of God , an order that spread rapidly across Europe and into the missionary world, still today devoted specifically to nursing the sick.
Canonized in 1690, John was declared patron of hospitals and the dying by Pope Leo XIII in 1886.
